newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SOCCER-ENGLAND AND GERMANY COME FACE-TO-FACE OFF THE FIELD.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-ENGLAND AND GERMANY COME FACE-TO-FACE OFF THE FIELD.

text.p: Ten months after their footballers met in the semifinals of the European championship, England and Germany come face-to-face again on Thursday in a very different setting.

This time their representatives will be wearing suits and ties rather than shirts and shorts and will have their exchange in a hotel meeting room rather than on the lush green turf of Wembley Stadium.

Delegates from the two countries will discuss with UEFA's executive committee how to progress with their respective bids for the right to host the 2006 World Cup, while trying to avoid a repeat of the unseemly in-fighting which marred the battle between Japan and South Korea for the 2002 edition.
No decisions will be taken at Thursday's meeting and neither side is due to make a formal presentation.
The meeting is primarily aimed at trying to resolve what approach should be taken towards securing the tournament for Europe in the face of rival bids from Africa and South America.
The main issue to be resolved is whether UEFA will back either Germany's or England's bid.
That simple idea became complicated three months ago when it emerged that Germany believed they had UEFA's support for their bid, which they signalled as long ago as 1993.
English officials expressed astonishment and said that just because Germany tabled their intentions first they should not have an advantage with UEFA.

No decision has to be taken on which bid to put forward until December 1998 and FIFA, world soccer's governing body, will not decide where the tournament is to be staged until June 2000. There is no guarantee that the tournament will even be in Europe.
UEFA's stance is to back just one country's bid to try to win the tournament for Europe. But there is nothing to stop the country which does not get UEFA's support taking their bid straight to FIFA.

Alec McGiven, the director of England's bid, told Reuters: "It is something of a red herring that just because the Germans bid first they should get UEFA's approval. There was absolutely no way England could bid for the World Cup until after Euro 96. England could only enter a bid once we proved we could stage a tournament of that magnitude successfully."
McGiven is keen to avoid getting into a bidding war with the Germans, as the Japanese and South Koreans did.
FIFA decided that Japan and South Korea would jointly stage the 2002 World Cup but ruled out joint hosts for future editions.
"There is no way we are going to run an anti-German campaign and spend hundreds of millions of pounds promoting our bid and criticising them," said McGiven.

"We do not want this to go completely out of control as it did between Japan and Korea. We intend to run an extremely effective, efficient campaign to get the point across that we should win the right to stage the tournament."
Officials from both England and Germany are known to be unhappy with UEFA for creating what they perceive to be an unnecessary problem.
On top of that, the Germans are unhappy with the English.
They feel that because they supported England's bid to stage last year's European championship, the English should support Germany's bid for the World Cup.

Wolfgang Niersbach, spokesman for the German Football Association (DFB) said: "We supported the English bid for Euro 96 and the re-admittance of English clubs back into Europe after the Heysel Stadium disaster. We expected their support for the 2006 World Cup but we will not go to FIFA if UEFA back England as that could split the European vote."
